title: Literary Classics Before 1900
summary: Audio-first study of influential pre-1900 literature, with complete narrative sequences and analyses from Dante and Shakespeare to Austen, the Brontës, Goethe, Milton, Chaucer, Boccaccio, Eliot, Tolstoy, and Dostoevsky.
assumed_background: No prior reading is needed for story lectures; critical lectures assume the narrated story or familiarity with the primary text.
Selections span medieval poetry, early modern drama and prose, Regency and Victorian fiction, Romantic Gothic narrative, mathematical satire, and French realism.
The Moby-Dick and Anna Karenina sections each narrate the complete principal plot before interpretive lectures, and name the English text or edition used for orientation.
Middlemarch follows eight books and a Finale; Crime and Punishment follows six parts and its epilogue. All story lectures precede the critical studies.

The Brontë sections use complete story sequences before literary analyses; Jane Eyre is first-person retrospective narration and Wuthering Heights is framed by Lockwood and Nelly Dean. No advance reading is required for the story lectures.
Goethe’s Faust is narrated in its entirety: Part One’s Gretchen tragedy and all five acts of Part Two; the two wagers and the competing final judgments are kept distinct.

Milton’s Paradise Lost is narrated book by book in the revised twelve-book 1674 arrangement, followed by interpretive lectures. The 1667 ten-book publication is separately identified; the poem is treated as poetry rather than scripture, and critiques are distinguished from the narrator’s positions.

Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales is treated as an unfinished collection of twenty-four tales in ten editorial fragments; every tale, the General Prologue, the Wife of Bath’s long prologue and the Retraction have individually narrated coverage. Narrative gaps are preserved, and interpretive questions follow the retellings.

Boccaccio’s Decameron narrative sequence covers all 100 tales and the complete plague frame, departure, and authorial epilogue (312000–423000). Lectures 424000–440000 provide historical and literary criticism with primary section links, evidence notes, and reception studies. Spoken word counts and durations are descriptive measurements, not targets.

Journey to the West has a separate World History complete-plot survey (048000–053000) and historical/textual study (054000). The expanded literary retelling currently narrates selected-witness chapters 1–63 in 48 continuous manuscripts; chapters 64–100 remain to be written. The chapter 9 family-origin narrative is an edition-sensitive insertion, and the numbering varies in other editions.
